messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Using older packages on newer R versions
messages.subject_clean: [D-RUG]: Using older packages on newer R versions
messages.body_plain:
Hey Matt,

A few thoughts, which may or may not help you:

 - You probably thought of this, but I didn't at first: when you run `update.packages`, make sure you include `checkBuilt=TRUE`, otherwise packages don't update to the new version of R.
 - I'm not sure if this would work, but I wonder if you can download the package source and build it yourself.  If there is some process that package authors need to initiate to make sure the binaries are updated, then maybe the sources are just fine if you build them locally.  Does anybody know more about this?
 - When you install a new version of R, by default it leaves the last version on your machine unless you delete it manually.  You can switch between the versions as needed.  Instructions here: http://www.rstudio.com/ide/docs/advanced/versions_of_r
 - An older version of R is probably good enough until the packages you want stop being compatible

Noam

Hi Greg,
Try the paste function.

> test=character(10)
> for (x in 1:10) { test[x] = paste("matrix-", x, ".Rdata", sep='')}
> test
 [1] "matrix-1.Rdata"  "matrix-2.Rdata"  "matrix-3.Rdata"  "matrix-4.Rdata"

Then just pass save() the variable test[x] inside the for loop where you'd usually specify a file string, ie:
save(dataset, file=test[x])

HTH,
Christopher Aden

Or, more concisely:

Note that this is ok only when concatenating parts of a file name. Directories should be combined with file.path, as this is more portable. For example:

file.path("test", paste0("matrix-", seq_len(10), ".Rdata"))

messages.body_plain:
Hi folks:

I was able to iterate within file names based on your answers to the last question I posted, so thanks again for the help with that. Now I have a bunch of .RData files that each store a 50 row x 38 column data array with column labels. I would like to set up a loop or some other kind of command to read each file back into the program and average them all together to yield a single averaged data array, as well as an additional array with some measure of variance for each entry. Files are saved in the format "matrix-[x].RData" and the array itself is called "dataset". Does anybody have any thoughts on functions that might be useful for setting this up? Thanks. My code is below if you'd like to take a look at it.

Greg

#Set seed value to generate same random numbers each time simulation is run
set.seed(9)

#Define number of times to run the simulation
last.run<-100

#Define length of each individual simulation run
last.decade<-50
n.decade<-last.decade+1

#Define number of file names to store for total number of simulation runs
test=character(last.run)

#Generate for loop to replicate model many times (comment out until model is complete)
for(x in 1:last.run){

#Generate data array for storing all relevant information per each simulation run
dataset<-array(0,c(n.decade,25))

#Assign names for each column; time steps, population sizes for each class and total population size,
#disease levels, dominant eigenvalues, stable stage distributions and reproductive values for each class
colnames(dataset)<-c("Decade","Cones","Seeds","Seedlings","Sm. saplings","Med. saplings","Large saplings",
                     "Mature trees","Total","Disease","Eigenvalue","SSD.C","SSD.S","SSD.1","SSD.2","SSD.3","SSD.4","SSD.5",
                     "RV.C","RV.S","RV.1","RV.2","RV.3","RV.4","RV.5")

#Define data array to store matrix at each time step for each run
data<-array(0,c(7,7,last.decade))

#Set up autoregressive model to simulate oscillating disease severity
#THIS IS TO BE REPLACED WITH DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS (I.E., LOTKA VOLTERRA)
b0=0.03
b1=-0.0005
b2=0.00025
b3=-0.0001
mean.P=matrix(0,1,n.decade)
mean.P[,1]=0.01
mean.P[,2]=0.04
mean.P[,3]=0.02
for (t in 4:n.decade){
  mean.P[,t]=b0+(b1+rnorm(1,0,0.1))*mean.P[,t-1]+(b2+rnorm(1,0,0.2))*mean.P[,t-2]+(b3+rnorm(1,0,0.2))*mean.P[,t-3]
}

#Initialize population vectors appropriate for the population projection matrix; The model will be assessed with
#seedbank alone (i.e., post stand clearing fire), seedlings alone (i.e., new plantation) and the stable stage distribution
#x.init<-c(0,100000,0,0,0,0,0)
#x.init<-c(0,0,1000,0,0,0,0)
x.init<-c(9009,90318,451,72,39,33,78)

#Assign column to store time step in decades
dataset[1:n.decade,1]<-1:n.decade

#Assign columns to store population size for each class
dataset[1,2:8]<-x.init

#Assign column to store total population size
dataset[1,9]<-sum(x.init)

#Assign column to store disease incidence
dataset[1:n.decade,10]<-mean.P[,1:n.decade]

#Assign column to store initial dominant eigenvalue
dataset[1,11]<-Re(which.max(eigen(matrix(c(
  0,0,0,1*(1-mean.P[,1]),16*(1-0.1*mean.P[,1]),70*(1-0.02*mean.P[,1]),74*(1-0.01*mean.P[,1]),
  10,0,0,0,0,0,0,
  0,0.00637*(1-mean.P[,1]),0,0,0,0,0,
  0,0,0.16*(1-mean.P[,1]),0,0,0,0,
  0,0,0,0.53*(1-0.1*mean.P[,1]),0.01,0,0,
  0,0,0,0,0.84*(1-0.05*mean.P[,1]),0.03,0,
  0,0,0,0,0,0.58,0.68
  ),7,7,byrow=T))[["values"]]))

#Assign columns to store initial stable stage distribution for each class
w<-Re(eigs.A[["vectors"]][,dom.pos])
ssd<-w/sum(w)
dataset[1,12:18]<-round(ssd,5)

#Assign columns to store initial reproductive values for each class
M<-eigen(t(A))
v<-Re(M$vectors[,which.max(Re(M$values))])
dataset[1,19:25]<-v/v[2]

#Iterate projection matrix over decades with disease parameters incorporated into affected stages/fecundities
for (t in 1:last.decade){
  A<-matrix(c(
    0,0,0,1*(1-mean.P[,t]),16*(1-0.1*mean.P[,t]),70*(1-0.02*mean.P[,t]),74*(1-0.01*mean.P[,t]),
    10,0,0,0,0,0,0,
    0,0.00637*(1-mean.P[,t]),0,0,0,0,0,
    0,0,0.16*(1-mean.P[,t]),0,0,0,0,
    0,0,0,0.53*(1-0.1*mean.P[,t]),0.01,0,0,
    0,0,0,0,0.84*(1-0.05*mean.P[,t]),0.03,0,
    0,0,0,0,0,0.58,0.68
    ),7,7,byrow=T)

  #Recalculate projection matrix at each time step and store in data frame
  data[,,t]<-A

  #Multiply previous time step population vector by current matrix to project population in next time step
  dataset[t+1,2:8]<-data[,,t]%*%dataset[t,2:8]

  #Calculate total population at each time step
  dataset[t+1,9]<-sum(dataset[t+1,2:8])

  #Calculate dominant eigenvalue for each time step and store to data set
  eigs.A<-eigen(A)
  dom.pos<-which.max(eigs.A[["values"]])
  L1<-Re(eigs.A[["values"]][dom.pos])
  dataset[t+1,11]<-L1

  #Calculate stable stage distribution to proportionally identify how many individuals per size class will
  #remain given each time step's matrix once oscillations have subsided
  w<-Re(eigs.A[["vectors"]][,dom.pos])
  ssd<-w/sum(w)
  dataset[t+1,12:18]<-round(ssd,5)

  #Calculate reproductive value to indicate each class's relative contribution to the future population
  M<-eigen(t(A))
  v<-Re(M$vectors[,which.max(Re(M$values))])
  dataset[t+1,19:25]<-v/v[2]

  #Close for-loop to complete iterations
}

#Set up a graph array to show three different graphs in one graphic
par(mfrow=c(1,3))

#Plot number of individuals per age class vs. decade w/ transposed matrices (for syntax of matplot, need to transpose population matrix)
matplot(1:n.decade,dataset[,2:8],type="l",ylim=c(0,max(dataset[,9])),xlab="Decades",ylab="Individuals",lwd=2,lty=1:6,pch=1,col=c(1:6,8),font=2,font.lab=2,cex.axis=2,cex.lab=2)

#Plot line on same graph for total population size
lines(1:n.decade,dataset[,9],type="l",pch=1,lty=9)

#Define legend to associate each line with representative class population
legend("topright",legend=c("Cones","Seeds","Seedlings","Small saplings","Med. saplings","Large saplings","Mature","Total"),lty=1:6,ncol=1,bty="n",col=c(1:6,8),cex=1.5);

#Plot number of individuals per age class vs. decade w/ transposed matrices at a smaller scale to better show details for saplings and mature trees
matplot(1:n.decade,dataset[,2:8],type="l",ylim=c(0,100),xlab="Decades",ylab="Individuals",lwd=2,lty=1:6,pch=1,col=c(1:6,8),font=2,font.lab=2,cex.axis=2,cex.lab=2)

#Define legend to associate each line with representative class population for the smaller-scaled graph
legend("topright",legend=c("Small saplings","Med. saplings","Large saplings","Mature"),lty=c(4:6,1),ncol=1,bty="n",col=c(4:6,8),cex=1.5);

#Calculate sensitivity matrix for final time step to indicate most important size classes for management
vw.s<-v%*%t(w)
(S<-vw.s/as.numeric(v%*%w))

#Calculate elasticity matrix for final time step to indicate most important size classes for management
elas<-(A/L1)*S
round(elas,3)

#Plot disease intensity over time
plot(1:n.decade,mean.P,xlab="Decades",ylab="Disease severity",type="l",font=2,cex.axis=2,cex.lab=2,font.lab=2)

#Design iteration for file names to generate new name for each simulation run
test[x]=paste("matrix-",x,".Rdata",sep='')

#Save the dataset from each simulation run using a different file name based on the previous step
save(dataset,file=test[x])

#Close for-loop to run simulation many times (comment out until model is complete)
}

#Display projection matrix at each time point with impact of pitch canker incorporated into parameters
data

#Display dataset head for current simulation run
head(dataset)

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

This week at D-RUG, I will run through how to set up a free cloud server through Amazon Web Services and run R and RStudio on it.  If you run anything in R that takes up lots of memory, or runs for a long time, running on AWS is super convenient.  Even if you don't require a high-power computer, an AWS server can be a second free computer on which to run code while freeing up your own computer for other tasks.

If you want to follow along step-by-step, you will need to sign up for an Amazon Web Services account ahead of time. Go to http://aws.amazon.com/ and click "Sign Up".  Note that, while we'll only be using services in the "free tier", AWS still requires credit card to create an account.  But Amazon likely has your credit card, anyway :)

See you at the regular time and place: Thursday, 1:10-3pm in Wickson 2124

Cheers,

Noam
